messages.body_plain:
Had 
I gone on a bit further, this would have been the next possibility, of 
course.

 

I'm 
inclined to think, though, that optim( ) provides a better general optimiser 
than nlminb( ) and I thought people should start to become aware of it.  It 
solves much more general problems than just fitting 
distributions.

 

Bill V.

>   What
>   about the fitdistr function in the MASS library (S-Plus 6.0 for
>   Windows)?  Seems to provide a very nice front-end to nlminb, with vcov
>   matrix estimated with vcov.nlminb of MASS:
>
>
>
>   >
>   fitdistr(y,dgamma,start=list(shape=4,rate=5))
>
>   shape
>   rate
>   4.044972
>   5.035894
>  (0.07821524) (0.1037563 )
>
>
>
>   (The
>   exact values naturally differ from Bill's because it's a different
>   sample.)
>
>
>
>   Brad
>
>   >     -----Original Message-----
> > From:
> >     Bill.Venables at CMIS.CSIRO.AU
> >     [mailto:Bill.Venables at CMIS.CSIRO.AU]
> > Sent: Saturday, September 28,
> >     2002 19:25 PM
> > To: wjcai2001 at hotmail.com;
> >     s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
> > Subject: Re: [S] fit the MLE of
> >     gamma dist
> >
> >
> >
> >     Let's take a bigger sample:
> >
> >
> >
> >     > y <- rgamma(5000, shape
> >     = 4, rate = 5)
> > > fm <- glm(y ~ 1, Gamma(link =
> >     identity))
> >
> >
> >     > library(MASS)
> >
> >     > shape <-
> >     gamma.shape(fm)$alpha
> > > rate <- shape/coef(fm)
> > > c(shape =
> >     shape, rate = as(rate,
> >     "vector"))
> >     shape     rate
> >
> >  4.016532 5.028475
> >
> >
> >
> >     Alternatively:
> >
> >
> >
> >     > gm <- ms(~
> >     -log(dgamma(y, shape = shape, rate = rate)),
> >
> >         start = c(shape=4,
> >     rate=5), trace = T)
> > > coef(gm)
> >
> >     shape     rate
> >  4.016532
> >     5.028475
> >
> >
> >
> >     Of course this is only half the story.  If you want
> >     standard errors you need to do a bit more work, but the information is there
> >     in the object fm and the output from gamma.shape(), which is part of the
> >     MASS library.
> >
> >
> >
> >     This is a fascinating simple problem and I could go on and on
> >     about it.  In fact I think I will.
> >
> >
> >
> >     In the MASS library for S-PLUS 6.x there is (courtesy of
> >     BDR) now a function optim() that not only optimises but optionally gets
> >     you a Hessian at the optimum.  So another way of finding the mle and
> >     getting an approximate variance matrix as well is as
> >     follows:
> >
> >
> >
> >     > fgamma <- function(par, y)
> >
> >             - sum(log(dgamma(y,
> >     shape = par[1], rate = par[2])))
> > > par <- c(shape = 4, rate =
> >     5)
> > > hm <- optim(par, fgamma, hessian = T, y = y)
> >
> > > se
> >     <- sqrt(diag(solve(hm$hessian)))  # don't forget to invert!
> > >
> >     cbind(hm$par,
> >     se)
> >
> >     se
> > shape 4.016415 0.07722422
> >  rate 5.028294

messages.subject: blank and missing graphs for lme residual plots
messages.subject_clean: blank and missing graphs for lme residual plots
messages.body_plain:
Thank you to Dr Renaud Lancelot and Dr. Jose Pinheiro for their responses 
(below) to my questions about how to view graphs I created following calls 
to lme, I am most appreciative.

Buzz Burhans

>  a graph page comes up,
> but it remains blank, though no error message appears, the object explorer
> does show that GSD2 has been created however. the command that results in
> this action is:
>
> residplot2 <- plot(preDMIlmetest2, form=resid(.,type = "p") ~ fitted(.) |
> TRT, abline = 0)
>

try:

print(residplot2)

All plot produced by the nlme library are trellis graphs, i.e. if you
store them in an object like you did above, they are not printed. It is
a useful feature when you want to combine several graphs on the same
page (see print.trellis).

Best,

Renaud

Dr Renaud Lancelot, vétérinaire

>  when I run the following command I get an error message:
>
> plot.ranef.lme(preDMIlmetest2)
>
> the error message is:
>
> > plot.ranef.lme(preDMIlmetest2)
> Error in [: No dim attribute for array subset: structure(..

The plot.ranef.lme method should be applied to a ranef.lme object (that is,
the object resulting from a call to ranef applied to an lme object) and not
directly to the lme object. You can try

> plot(ranef(preDMIlmetest2))

> Furthermore, when I run the following graph command, a graph page comes
up,
> but it remains blank, though no error message appears, the object
explorer
> does show that GSD2 has been created however. the command that results in
> this action is:
>
> residplot2 <- plot(preDMIlmetest2, form=resid(.,type = "p") ~ fitted(.) |
> TRT, abline = 0)

This is related to the way S works. The result of the call to plot, which
you would like to see appearing in the GSD2 window, is actually being saved
to the object residplot2. You can either call plot without saving the
result,

> plot(preDMIlmetest2, form=resid(.,type = "p") ~ fitted(.) | TRT, abline
= 0)

or you can print the object to get the plot

> print(residplot2)

Either way should work

Hope this helps.

Best,

--José

------------------------------------------------------------------

José Pinheiro

B

messages.subject: .Call interface and attaching/detaching library
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,

I am still trying to understand why calling C compiled
code with .Call interface does not work once the library
has been loaded and unloaded one or several times (S-PLUS 6.1,
Windows 2000): the called function does not return any value and
I am not even sure that it is called at all. For very simple examples,
the error occurs only when commands are run from a script :(.

Technical support at Insightful was able to reproduce the problem 
but did not provide any explanation (it's a bug!). I did not get
any reply from this list to my previous posts. 

In spite of the fact that I have encounted this problem everytime that
I have tried to use the .Call interface (see below), neither the 
developpers at Insightfull nor anybody on this list seems to have
encountered it before. Because I am lost, I would greatly appreciate
any answer to the following questions:

Has anybody succeeded using the .Call interface in
a library that could be detached and reattached several
times without problem (from a script as well as from the
command windows)?

If yes, could somebody give me a simple example of code that works?

I have tried the examples in the Programmer's Guide (makeseq example, p.
682) and V&R's S Programming book (e.g convolve2 example, p.142) without 
success. Even the simple project that is automatically created when one uses 
the S-PLUS wizard to create a DLL in VC++ can lead to this 
problem. Note that in that with these simple examples, one needs 
to run commands that detaches, reattaches and calls the function 
from a script window several times in order to get the error. More
complex functions using .Call stop working immediately 
after the library has been detached and reattached and it does
not matter whether the commands came from the script or commands window. 
I would be glade to give more info if anyone is interested. 

Thank you for your attention,

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

messages.subject: Re: merge data.frames by timeDate
messages.body_plain:
I have to agree with Eric Zivot that the new timeDate class can be 
extremely useful, and with Wim Kimmerer that it can be mysterious and 
frustrating.

Part of the reason for the frustrating nature of the timeDate class is that 
it is an S4 class.  timeDate vectors do not work with many of the core 
language features of S3, such as c(), unlist(), for() (e.g., if you try to 
use c() to concatentate two timeDate vectors, you get gibberish.)

timeDate vectors can be used as columns in data frames, but if you want to 
do anything with the data frame other than index and subset it, expect 
problems (note also that such usage falls outside the somewhat obscure 
original definition of a dataframe).  It is also possible to use a timeDate 
vector as the row names of a data frame, but in my experience this is 
definitely to be avoided because of the nasty problems that crop up.  For 
both columns and row names of data frames, it's often better to convert the 
timeDate vector to a character data vector and then use that (for columns 
you might want to further convert it to a factor, which would allow you to 
be fully conformant with the strict definition of a dataframe).

-- Tony Plate

At 02:42 AM 9/29/2002 -0700, Eric Zivot wrote:
> I agree that the timeDate objects can be mysterious at first. Insightful's
> manual description of these objects is a bit confusion. And, Insightful
> does not make clear which functions operate correctly on them and which do
> not. For merging data on timeDate, I recommend creating timeSeries objects
> and then using the function seriesMerge. I don't think this works at the
> gui level (I keep bugging Insightful to improve the gui support for
> timeSeries objects). Also, you do have to be careful about time zone
> issues and I recommend setting the time zone to GMT using the options
> command to avoid any strangeness. In S-PLUS 6 for windows, the time zone
> of the timeDate object was set according to the windows regional setting.
> In S-PLUS 6.1, I believe the default is now GMT.
>
>
>
> However, after figuring out how they work I found the new time series
> objects (timeDate and timeSeries) to be extremely powerful and useful,
> especially for dealing with high frequency financial data. My recent book,
> Modeling Financial Time Series with S-PLUS, Springer 2002, emphasizes the
> usefulness of the new time series objects in S-PLUS 6. See, in particular,
> chapter 2 on time series specification, manipulation and visualization.
>
>
>
> Unfortunately, Insightful has not integrated the new timeSeries objects
> into all of the statistical fitting functions. However, you can always
> strip away the timeDate information of a timeSeries by extracting the data
> using the seriesData function. The new S+FinMetrics module I helped
> develop is built around the new timeSeries objects and all of the
> functions work correctly with timeDate and timeSeries objects.
>
>
>
> If you work a lot with time series data, I wouldn't give up on the
> timeDate and timeSeries objects. They are extremely powerful and useful.
>
>
>
> ez
> On Sat, 28 Sep 2002, Wim Kimmerer wrote:
>
> > Dave, I have found timeDate to be so mysterious and klunky that I have
>
> > given up on it (Splus 6.0, but I think it is the same).  Merge, graphs, and
>
> > quite a few other operations that should be straightforward give you
>
> > garbage.  I wrote a few simple functions to compute year , month, and day
>
> > (NOT as factors, which even SPlus 2000 returned for some reason, but as
>
> > numbers) and use those to merge.  A lot of my data are daily so I don't
>
> > care about the time, but I think it has something to do with time zones.
>
> > The transition between daylight time and standard time will catch you too.
>
> >
>
> > My suggestion in Splus 6.x is to avoid timeDate for most numerical
> operations.
>
> >
>
> > Wim
>
> >
>

Dear Kenneth,

In S4 (e.g., S-Plus 6 for Windows), n <- 5000 is stored as an integer, and 
n*n*n is too big, producing an overflow. Setting n <- 5000. (i.e., with a 
decimal point) causes n to have storage mode double, and the computation 
succeeds.

I hope that this helps,
 John

You can coerce a variable to real; here are two examples:

        > cube <- function(x) as.double(x)^3
        > cube(5000)
        [1] 1.25e+011

integers, but causing users to think about the storage mode of numbers 
seems to me to be a trap that it's easy to fall into.

 John

I realized that I screwed up the example (since ^ coerces to real anyway).

The general point is that if at least one number in a computation is real,

 John

messages.subject: Summary: merge data.frames by timeDate
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Wim Kimmerer, Eric Zivot, Tony Plate, and Frank Harrell Jr. for
taking time to answer my question.  Part of Tony's response was the most
helpful and informative:

timeDate vectors can be used as columns in data frames, but if you want to
do anything with the data frame other than index and subset it, expect
problems (note also that such usage falls outside the somewhat obscure
original definition of a dataframe).  It is also possible to use a timeDate

vector as the row names of a data frame, but in my experience this is
definitely to be avoided because of the nasty problems that crop up.  For
both columns and row names of data frames, it's often better to convert the

timeDate vector to a character data vector and then use that (for columns
you might want to further convert it to a factor, which would allow you to
be fully conformant with the strict definition of a dataframe).

I agree that timeDate vectors restrict the definition of a data.frame.
Unfortunately, the Grid Editor sets data.frames with dates vectors to read
only.  I see absolutely no reason for that except to force users to us
timeDate rather than dates.  That is very unfortunate because dates vectors
do not restrict the definition of a data.frame. Insightful should remove
that restriction on the Grid Editor.

Incidentally, I was able to merge the data sets on the timeDate columns.  I
discovered that the critical piece is the display format.  I discovered it
when I converted the columns to character and those also failed to merge.
Upon some examination, I discovered that in one data.frame, an extra space
was appended to the date string.  Apparently, the output format is
important in merging on timeDate columns. I verified that setting the
output format to be the same does work.  I cannot use the "Change
Properties" dialog because nothing shows up in the Time Zone box and it
refuses to do anything.  However, I can set the format slot of the column
using the command line.

Dave

messages.subject: timeDate objects
messages.body_plain:
I'm a little late to this discussion, but would like to add some
observations/opinions.

  1. I first encountered timeDate objects in the beta of S5.0, and there
were a lot more problems with them at that time.  Most of the problems
that I found were fixed, and I think that most of the problems that were
mentioned in these recent discussions could be also.

  2. An advantage of the new class structure is fine control: you can
specify what should happen with "timeDate + integer", with implicit
conversions of timeDate to other object types, and etc.  The original
designer of timeDates had time series computations in mind, and used those
features of the new class structure to add some useful functionality to
the class.

  3. In my experience with the new classes, one problem is that one ends
up having to specify behavior for almost everything.  For instance, in
the first iteration of timeDate, the expression
        age <- (timeDate(today) - timeDate(birthdate))/ 365.25
gave an unexpected result.  This is because, given the set of rules that
the class had about conversions, it made a guess as to what one wanted
here, and guessed wrong.  We want a simple floating point, it gave me a
weird timeSpan object.  Once pointed out to the developer, she said
(more or less) "Oh.  I never thought of that example.", then added a rule
to fix it.

  The current timeDate does the wrong thing in several cases.  The behavior
can probably be fixed.

  4. I personally find the new class structure to be more trouble than it
is worth for most things, and have used it for only 1 serious effort.
There is wide, almost religious difference of opinion on this.  When they
are finally "done" and all glitches programmed out, timeDates will likely
be an example case for the use of S4 classes.  

I do wish  new classes had two more features:
  a. A "fallback" rule.  For simple dates, for instance: "if you are at
all unsure or confused, turn it into an integer".  This approach is
almost antithetical to the philosophical views of some, but would prevent
a lot of grief for day-to-day users.
  b. One particular fallback, for all object: the ability for a user to
add an arbitrary collection of attributes.  The object would retain the
same class, but with a fallback of "drop the user-attributes".

  Both are a reflection of my experience with adding things to S -- I am
never even CLOSE to forseeing all the uses and actions that others will
find for my additions.  S4 classes have some neat features, but require
more maintainance.

        Terry Therneau

Whether you?re a beginner or seasoned professional, our training services can 
help you improve your analytic skills. We offer public and private courses to 
meet your specific training requirements. Learn about the latest trends, 
methods and more from industry gurus and academic leaders. Hands-on training 
courses offer you an opportunity to apply your knowledge.

Here is a list of upcoming training courses. Click on the links to view the 
detailed course description, prerequisites, course objectives, and location 
info.

S-PLUS Essentials: Command Line: Oct. 22-25, 2002 in San Francisco, CA
click here for all details: http://www.insightful.com/services/course.asp?CID=10
This hands-on training course is designed for users new to S-PLUS 6. This 
course provides a full range of command line operations for data manipulation, 
graphing, statistics and statistical models, and function writing in the S-PLUS 
language. An optional fourth day will introduce the graphical user interface, a 
powerful tool for rapid access to the many features of the S-PLUS 6 program 
environment. Even committed command line users will be surprised by the depth 
and ease of use in the new S-PLUS 6 graphical user interface. 

Statistical Modeling in S-PLUS: October 28-30, 2002 in San Francisco, CA
click here for all details: http://www.insightful.com/services/course.asp?CID=11
This three-day course covers the modeling methods available with the latest 
version of S-PLUS. We present a brief introduction and background of several 
modeling methods, which include linear, ANOVA, generalized linear, generalized 
additive, tree based, nonlinear, mixed effects, and survival models. Using real 
world data, we will focus on fitting a model and interpreting the results. A 
brief introduction to model fitting at the graphical user interface provides an 
illustration of the ease with which model fitting can be done in this 
environment.

Presented by Dr. Jose' Pinheiro
click here for all details: http://www.insightful.com/services/course.asp?CID=19
Mixed-effects models provide a powerful tool for analyzing grouped data, 
because they model flexibly the within-group correlation often present in this 
type of data. Examples of grouped data include repeated measures, longitudinal 
data, multilevel data, and some split-plot experiments, being collected in a 
wide variety of areas. This two-day course describes how to fit and analyze 
linear and nonlinear mixed-effects models in S-PLUS, using the recently 
released NLME 3.3 software. This is an applied course, with emphasis on real 
life examples to motivate and illustrate the use of mixed-effects models.

messages.subject: Re: timeDate and S4 classes
messages.body_plain:
>>>>> "FH" == Frank E Harrell <fharrell at virginia.edu> writes:
  FH> I am using R now to do a few things that can't be done in S-Plus,
  FH> related to adding attributes to simple objects and related to multiple
  FH> inheritance. I sincerely hope that R does not make the same decisions as
  FH> S-Plus. I would like for this code to keep working in at least one
  FH> system.

At least with R you don't have to "upgrade" to a new version that isn't
backward compatible.

SV4 classes are an abomination.  If you want to know how to do objects, look
at Smalltalk.  Everything is an object (i.e., an instance of a class), you can
look at and modify any class, and your own classes and objects are on the same
footing as the ones that came with the system.  Polymorphism, inheritance,
operator overloading, it's all there, along with development tools that put
every other language to shame.  At the same time, Smalltalk is one of the
simplest and easiest languages in existence.  Only five keywords.  Google for
VWNC (VisualWorks Non-Commercial) for a really nice implementation that you
can use noncommercially for free, or browse over to www.whysmalltalk.com for
more info about all dialects.

The biggest problem with SV4 is one it shares with C++, Java, and several
other languages: it's a hybrid of object and non-object concepts.  The two
paradigms do not mix well.  Another problem is that at the same time, SV4
tries to do way too much for a language with roots in the scripting world.
Multiple inheritance introduces more complexity than it is worth, and multiple
dispatch (i.e., signatures) means that methods do not belong to classes but
somehow float about on their own.  While the language is now more powerful, it
is much less forgiving and far more complicated. 

I tried to work with the new time series objects when they first came out in
S5, but I gave up after a very short time.  I have a lot of code written to
use my own time series classes, and for my purposes my own stuff is better
suited.  

Working with classes does require you to think a little bit about what you are
doing.  Terry Therneau complained about the expression

        age <- (timeDate(today) - timeDate(birthdate))/ 365.25

giving an unexpected result, namely a timeSpan object. He wanted the result to
be a simple floating point number giving age in years.  One problem with
Terry's answer is that it implicitly assumes that the underlying units are
days, not seconds, milliseconds, months or years.  Of course the difference
between two timeDates should be a timeSpan, and dividing a timeSpan by a
number should yield another timeSpan.  What's missing here is something to
convert a timeSpan to years.  In Smalltalk, the above expression would look
something like this:

age := ((TimeDate today - (TimeDate fromYmd: 19900328))/365.25) lengthInYears.

or

age := (TimeDate today - (TimeDate fromYmd: 19900328)) lengthInDays / 365.25.

In either case, it's quite clear what's going on.  In S, you'd have something
like:
 
        age <- ((timeDate(today) - timeDate(birthdate)) @ .Data)[[1]] / 365.25
 
or something even worse.  Note that my use of [[1]] relies on a particular slot
position, which is really bad form.  But in a few minutes of dinking around I
couldn't find a julian() or days() function that would return the number of
days in a timeSpan. In Smalltalk, methods that operate on instances of a class
belong to that class and are easily found by just browsing the class.  So my
hypothetical lengthInDays method would be found in the hypothetical TimeSpan
class (there is no such class in Smalltalk, although the ANSI standard does
call for a Duration class, which is similar), while 'today' and 'fromYmd:'
would be class methods in TimeDate.

I urge anyone interested in pain-free programming to look into Smalltalk.

Jeff Hallman

messages.subject: Re: timeDate and S4 classes
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-list,

I use timeDate, timeSpan, and timeSeries at a regular basis for handling
(highly) irregular timeSeries and I do think that IT WORKS VERY WELL, the
exceptions being that plotting highly irregular timeSeries don't always
work.  Also the use of global options are somewhat disturbing. 

It is nice that a expression like 

(timeDate(today) - timeDate(birthdate)) / 365.25

is handled in a "logical" way, but you could argue that the above does
not make sense simply because it relies on a timeSpan being coerced into
the number of days.   Why not expect that

(timeDate(today) - timeDate(birthdate)) / 864000

results in the age in days? (As it would in C). When trying to handle all
these special cases the programming and maintenance gets complicated.  It
seems more logical to use:

(timeDate(today) - timeDate(birthdate)) / timeSpan("365 days 6 hours")

Regards,
Henrik

messages.subject: S and macros
messages.body_plain:
I know that S has a variety of functionality that allows you to
compute on the language itself like deparse, substitute etc.  So you
can compute expressions, evaluate them, etc.  I was wondering if
anyone has used that to develop any sort of substitution macro
facility in S or R.  I was hoping for something as powerful as
defmacro/backquote in lisp, but even something with the minimal
functionality of define/cpp as used in C would be helpful.

Here are two sample cases to illustrate the flavor of the problems I
would like to address:

1.  Frequently I want to return a list of objects, and have the list
    names match the objects, i.e.

    list(obj1=obj1,
         obj2=obj2,
         obj3=obj3)

    etc.

    This is redundant, prone to typo/cut/paste errors if names are
    similar (i.e. an obj3=obj2 might sneak in), prone to error not
    caught by the S parser if commas are missing, etc.  Certainly you
    could write something in S to construction the expression above
    and then evaluate it, or to assign names after the fact, but I'm
    looking for something more pattern based that would address this
    and other issues as well.

    This kind of thing can be defined more elegantly with lisp
    backquote, but even cpp can do something useful:

    #define doubleup(x) x=x
    list(doubleup(obj1),
         doubleup(obj2),
         doubleup(obj3))

    Or in a bizarre combination of S, C, and Lisp:
    #define doubleup(x) x=x
    #define namedlist(objects) list(,@lapply(objects,doubleup)
    namedlist(obj1,obj2,obj3)

2. Perhaps you have written a large function and you recognize that
   some sections of it are near copies of each other and should be
   abstracted out to a new subfunction.  You might find that the
   section you are abstracting has many ties via many variables to the
   environment of the parent, and everyone of them must be passed down
   to the subfunction (as well as the possible fun of dealing with the
   semantics of "...").  Below is a trivial example using + (pretend
   instead that it does something complicated, not something simple
   and commutative like +; perhaps it is a simulation depending on all
   5 args or something), you might start out with this in the big
   function body:

     #pretend each line is really 50 lines of code doing a complicated
     #simulation that depends on all 5 of its inputs
     a <- a + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5
     b <- b + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5

   If that took up 100 lines of code, you might instead turn it into 2
   lines and then a 50 line function that gets used twice:

     a <- subfunc(a,temp2,temp3,temp4,temp5)
     b <- subfunc(b,temp2,temp3,temp4,temp5)

     subfunc <- function(x,temp2,temp3,temp4,temp5) {
        x + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5
     }

   This can certainly shorten the function and reduce the amount of
   code that appears twice, since it is abstracted into subfunc.
   However, it requires you to define subfunc with all those args, and
   in editing to create subfunc there are many cut/paste errors you
   might make (leaving a.temp1 in place).  Some cut/paste errors get
   caught at run time when the variable is undefined, but others might
   find a value and return a bad result.

   I would rather do something involving text/rewriting/macro where
   the function call semantics do not come into play, i.e.

     #define pattern(x) x <- x + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5
     pattern(a)
     pattern(b)

Any suggestions?  Maybe these kinds of things can be done easily in S
without adding anything as bulky as a function library implementing
some kind of substitution macro, and I'm just not thinking about this
the right way?

Thanks.

--garyg

Delphi Capital Management |  FAX:      (781) 647-7779
10 Carroll Circle         |  Internet: gary at sabot.com
Weston, MA 02493  USA     |  
-------------------------------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
An answer to your question 1  I think is:

s.doubleup<-function(...)
{
        out<-list(...)
        names(out)<-unlist(sys.call())[-1]
        out
}

Input is names of your objects; return is named list with your objects as
components

For your question 2, I suspect something like deparse(substitute()) might be
most of it, since you essentially want to turn an expression into a
character vector. But maybe it's more involved.

messages.subject: plot.timeSeries skips weekends
messages.body_plain:
Just a note to save others (who are not stock market analysts) aggravation:
I discovered to my surprise that when using the function plot.timeSeries,
the default on the time axis is NOT to plot data that fall on weekends.
This is not mentioned anywhere in the documentation--it is caused by a
parameter called "skip.weekends" whose default value is True, which is part
of the confusing and poorly documented "axis.time" function that sets up the
x-axis.  Other aspects of the axis.time function don't work correctly.  For
instance,
plot.timeSeries(data, xaxis.args=list(skip.weekends=F,by.label="days"))
will fail to label the axis correctly; this is a bug Insightful is aware of.

John Payne

par(mfrow=c(3,1))
plot(x1); plot(x2); plot(x1, x2)

messages.subject: GLM AIC question
messages.body_plain:
Hello listmembers-

I am using glm to do logisitic regression.  I would like to calculate the
AIC of the fitted models that I have.  I checked the help files for AIC and
GLM in S, and although AIC doesnt seem to operate with GLM (I checked by
trying it also), GLM does return the deviance.  In the GLM help for
glm.object this is defined as -2 times the maximum likelihood.  Exactly what
one wants for the AIC.

However, I read McCullagh and Nelder (the background reference listed for
GLM) to check what the deviance actually is, and in the book they define it
as the difference between the maximum likelihood fit for a model and the
maximum likelihood achievable (i.e. if the fitted values for each
observation match the observation exactly, page 118).  The McCullagh and
Nelder definition is for the residual deviance - but they refer to this as
the deviance.  So, does anyone know if Splus is calculating the deviance or
the residual deviance, and if its the residual deviance if there is an easy
way to extract the deviance itself.  Or, maybe more directly to just get the
AIC for the model?

Thanks for the help,

Chris

Subject: RE: [S] strange printing after c(runif(2), x)
From: "David Smith" <dsmith at insightful.com>

"if" statements have a value -- the value of the clause indicated 
by the logical expression.  In your case it's the value of the 
expression "x <- c(runif(3),x)", a sequence of random numbers.

The autoprinter only suppresses printing of the value of 
assignment expressions (technically, expressions of mode "<-"), 
but your statement is an expression of mode "if"; it therefore 
does get autoprinted.  Note that "if (T) 1" also gets 
autoprinted.

# David Smith

messages.body_plain:
A big 
thank-you to Bill Dunlap at Insightful who just made my

life a 
little easier.  His code for spreading the labels 
follows.

That is 
exactly what I needed.  Anyone who uses image plots

should 
know about it.  

 

Thanks 
also to Sundar Dorai-Raj, Jan Brogger, Naomi Altman, and 

Bert 
Gunter who all replied with helpful suggestions.

 

 Myong-Hee

 

[Bill 
Dunlap's 
message]------------------------------------------------------

Is this the sort of thing you are looking for? Call it like 
axis()

and adjust the 'spread.factor' to some pleasing amount. 'line' 
specifies

how far away from the plot the labels should be.

"spread.axis" <-

function(side, at, labels, ticks = F, line = 2, ..., 
spread.factor = 2)

{

ylim <- par("usr")[3:4] # y limits of plot in user 
units.

xlim <- par("usr")[1:2] # x limits ...

cxy <- par("cxy") # size of character in user 
units

if(side == 4 || side == 2) {

# y axis

center <- sum(ylim)/2

spread.at <- center + (at - center) * 
spread.factor

mtext(text = paste(" ", labels, sep = ""), side = side, line 
=

line, at = spread.at, adj = if(side == 2) 1 else 0,

...)

segments(xpd = T, x1 = if(side == 2) xlim[1] else 
xlim[2],

x2 = if(side == 2) xlim[1] - line * cxy[1] else xlim[

2] + line * cxy[1], y1 = at, y2 = spread.at)

} else {

stop("Code not written for x axis")

}

}

E.g.,

par(mfrow=c(5,1), oma=c(0,0,0,20))

plot(1:10, axes=F)

box()

axis(side=1)

spread.axis(side=4, at=1:10, 
labels=paste("Number",1:10))

messages.subject: Re: results not equals
messages.body_plain:
Dear Francisco,

At 02:18 PM 10/5/2002 -0300, Francisco Cysneiros wrote:

> I'm using Splus 2000 release 3 and I found this situation
> > y<--2.42
> > x<--2.42
> > x^y
> [1] NA
> > -2.42^-2.42
> [1] -0.1178058
> Why NA ? This two results should be equals !
>
> Please someone tell me about this problem .

I believe that I recall a similar problem recently posted to this list (or 
maybe it was the R list). In any event, the reason that you're getting a 
result in the second case, but NA in the first, is that exponentiation has 
higher precedence than negation:

        > -2.42^-2.42
        [1] -0.117805838
        > -(2.42^-2.42)
        [1] -0.117805838
        > (-2.42)^-2.42
        [1] NA

If you want a complex result, then you should coerce the numbers to 
complex; for example,

        > as.complex(-2.42)^-2.42
        [1] 0.0292971207-0.114104751i
        > (-2.42)^as.complex(-2.42)
        [1] 0.0292971207-0.114104751i

I hope that this helps,
 John

messages.subject: Summary of responses on S and macros
messages.subject_clean: Summary of responses on S and macros
messages.body_plain:
I received several very helpful responses to my question about macros,
so I thought I'd summarize the results to the list.  

----------------

Andy Liaw pointed me to Thomas Lumley's Programmers Niche column
(http://cran.r-project.org/doc/Rnews/Rnews_2001-3.pdf) which
implements a defmacro function for R.  Thats pretty much exactly what
I was looking for.  Thomas then sent me a few extensions for it, and I
tried with partial success (at the bottom of this email) to convert it
to S from R.

Also, Thomas solved my dbl problem with a function, no macro required:

    dbl<-function(...){
        args<-list(...)
        tags<-sapply(substitute(list(...)),deparse)[-1]
        names(args)<-tags
        args
    }
    
    so that
      dbl(alpha,beta,gamma)
    is equivalent to
      list(alpha=alpha,beta=beta,gamma=gamma)
    
Bert Gunter came up with something similar:

    s.doubleup<-function(...)
    {
        out<-list(...)
        names(out)<-unlist(sys.call())[-1]
        out
    }
    
----------------
    
Patrick Burns reminded me that S Poetry covers some ideas that are
applicable to the same problem (http://www.seanet.com/~pburns/Spoetry
and http://www.i-way.co.uk/~pat/Spoetry)

----------------
Tim Hesterberg had a few pointers that are useful for this kind of
macro programming:

   (1) Create an expression, then eval() it.  You can use
   expressions in many of the places that you probably currently
   use functions.  Expressions can be hundreds of lines long, inside {}.
   
   (2) Use substitute() to modify an expression.
   
   For an extended example, do
        library(missing)
   then look at how miEval works.  Basically if you do
        miEval(myExpression, could be hundreds of lines long)
   miEval creates modified versions of myExpression and evaluates them.
   
----------------
Chuck Taylor uses a different approach based on manipulating strings
rather than expressions:

    I tend to favor using various string-manipulation functions to
    construct S expressions as strings, then evaluating them using the
    eval(parse(text=...)) trick.  I have included below a few short S
    functions inspired by your examples.  Here are some illustrations
    of their use:
    
    > names
     [1] "obj1"  "obj2"  "obj3"  "obj4"  "obj5"  "obj6"  "obj7" 
     [8] "obj8"  "obj9"  "obj10"
    > doubleup(names)
     [1] "obj1 = obj1"   "obj2 = obj2"   "obj3 = obj3"  
     [4] "obj4 = obj4"   "obj5 = obj5"   "obj6 = obj6"  
     [7] "obj7 = obj7"   "obj8 = obj8"   "obj9 = obj9"  
    [10] "obj10 = obj10"
    > combine(names, names, sep="=")
     [1] "obj1=obj1"   "obj2=obj2"   "obj3=obj3"   "obj4=obj4"  
     [5] "obj5=obj5"   "obj6=obj6"   "obj7=obj7"   "obj8=obj8"  
     [9] "obj9=obj9"   "obj10=obj10"
    > makelist(names)
    [1] "(obj1 = obj1, obj2 = obj2, obj3 = obj3, obj4 = obj4, obj5 = obj5, obj6 
= obj6, 
    obj7 = obj7, obj8 = obj8, obj9 = obj9, obj10 = obj10)"
    
    > charvector <- "x <- x + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5"
    > replaceAll("x", "a", charvector)
    [1] "a <- a + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5"
    > replaceAll("x", "b", charvector)
    [1] "b <- b + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5"
    
    > cs2
    [1] "x <- x + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5"
    [2] "y <- y + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5"
    > replaceAll("temp", "ABC", cs2)
    [1] "x <- x + ABC2 + ABC3 + ABC4 + ABC5"
    [2] "y <- y + ABC2 + ABC3 + ABC4 + ABC5"
    
    Using paste() can help a lot too:
    
    > paste(names, collapse=" + ")
    [1] "obj1 + obj2 + obj3 + obj4 + obj5 + obj6 + obj7 + obj8 + obj9 + obj10"
    
    Here is an example of using eval(parse(text=...)) in combination
    with one of the above functions:
    
    First note that
    
    > combine(names, 1:10, " <- ")
     [1] "obj1 <- 1"   "obj2 <- 2"   "obj3 <- 3"   "obj4 <- 4"  
     [5] "obj5 <- 5"   "obj6 <- 6"   "obj7 <- 7"   "obj8 <- 8"  
     [9] "obj9 <- 9"   "obj10 <- 10"
    
    This produces a vector of S expressions.  We can parse and
    evaluate these expressions in one step:
    
        eval(parse(text=combine(names, 1:10, " <- ")))
    
    Note then that, for example, 
    
    > obj3
    [1] 3
    
    
    The function definitions follow.
    
    "doubleup" <- 
    # Create a charvector of the form "x = x"
    function(x) {
        paste(x, "=", x)
    }
    
    "makelist" <-
    # doubleup and make into comma-separated list in parentheses
    function(x) {
       paste("(", paste(doubleup(x), collapse=", "), ")", sep="")
    }
    
    "combine" <- 
    # Create a character vector, each element of which is the
    #   concatenation of the corresponding elements of the 
    #   leftside and rightside vectors, separated by "separator"
    function(leftside, rightside, separator) {
        if(length(leftside) != length(rightside)) 
        stop("leftside and rightside have unequal lengths")
        paste(leftside, rightside, sep = separator)
    }
    
    #new version with bug fixes, which chuck emailed me later on:
    "replaceAll" <-
    # Replace each occurrence of string1 with string2 
    # in a vector of character strings
    function(string1, string2, charvector)
    {
        positions <- regMatchPos(charvector, string1)
        while(any(!is.na(positions[, 1]))) {
                substring(charvector, positions[, 1], positions[, 2]) <- string2
#               substring(charvector, positions[1, 1],  positions[1, 2]) <- 
string2
                positions <- regMatchPos(charvector, string1)
        }
        charvector
    }
----------------

Below I include Thomas Lumley's defmacro, to which I made some minor
changes (so any bugs are mine), plus a conversion to S that doesn't
totally work (if the macro uses local variables, the call to remove
them is having trouble finding them, but it isn't clear to me that it
matters given how gensym works).

#Based on Thomas Lumley's article in the Programmer's Niche column on
#http://cran.r-project.org/doc/Rnews/Rnews_2001-3.pdf
#Plus email followups with tlumley at u.wsahington.edu
#to add local variables

.R. <- F

if(.R.) {
   gensym <- function(base=".v.",envir=parent.frame()){
      repeat{
         nm<-paste(base,paste(sample(letters,7,replace=TRUE),
                              collapse=""),sep=".")
         if (!exists(nm,envir=envir))
            break
      }
      as.name(nm)
   }

} else {

   gensym <- function(base=".v.",envir=sys.parent(1)){
      repeat{
         nm<-paste(base,paste(sample(letters,7,replace=TRUE),
                              collapse=""),sep=".")
         if (!exists(nm,where=envir))
            break
      }
      as.name(nm)
   }
}

if(.R.) {

defmacro <-function(...,expr,local=NULL){
  expr<-substitute(expr)
  a<-substitute(list(...))[-1]
  nn<-names(a)
  if (is.null(nn)) nn<-rep("",length(a))
  for(i in seq(length=length(a))){
    if (nn[i]=="") {
      nn[i]<-paste(a[[i]])
      msg<-paste(a[[i]],"not supplied")
      a[[i]]<-substitute(stop(foo),list(foo=msg))
    }
  }
  names(a)<-nn
  a<-as.list(a)

  if(is.null(local)) {
     ff<-eval(substitute(function(){
        tmp<-substitute(body)
        eval(tmp,parent.frame())
     },list(body=expr)))
  } else {
     ff<-eval(substitute(function(){
        tmp<-substitute(body)
        locals<-lapply(local,gensym,envir=parent.frame())
        names(locals)<-local
        tmp<-do.call("substitute",list(tmp,locals))
        rval<-eval(tmp,parent.frame())
        rm(list=as.character(locals),envir=parent.frame())
        rval
     },list(body=expr)))
  }

  formals(ff)<-a
  mm<-match.call()
  mm$expr<-NULL
  mm[[1]]<-as.name("macro")
  attr(ff,"source")<-c(deparse(mm),deparse(expr))
  ff
}

} else {

defmacro <- function(..., expr,local=NULL){
   expr <- substitute(expr)
   a <- substitute(list(...))[-1]
   ## process the argument list
   nn <- names(a)
   if (is.null(nn)) nn <- rep("", length(a))
   for(i in seq(length=length(a))) {
      if (nn[i] == "") {
         nn[i] <- paste(a[[i]])
         msg <- paste(a[[i]], "not supplied")
         a[[i]] <- substitute(stop(foo),
                              list(foo = msg))
      }
   }
   names(a) <- nn
   a <- as.list(a)

   ## this is where the work is done
   #S version, function is a list of args ending in body
   ff <- a
   if(is.null(local)){
      ff[[length(ff)+1]] <- substitute(
                                       {
                                          tmp <- substitute(body)
                                          eval(tmp, sys.parent(1))
                                       },
                                       list(body = expr))
   } else {
      ff[[length(ff)+1]] <- substitute(
                                       {
                                          tmp <- substitute(body)
                                          
locals<-lapply(local,gensym,envir=sys.parent(1))
                                          names(locals) <- local
                                          tmp <- 
do.call("substitute",list(tmp,locals))
                                          rval <- eval(tmp, sys.parent(1))
                                          #when macro is run at top level, 
where=1, this breaks?
#                                          
remove(list=as.character(locals),where=sys.parent(1))
#kludge for now, so top level works.  Beneath that, it generates clutter
#till the function/frame exits
                                          vars.to.kill <- as.character(locals)
                                          if(exists(vars.to.kill[1])) 
remove(list=vars.to.kill)
                                          rval
                                       },
                                       list(body = expr,local=local))
   }
      
   ff <- as.function(ff)

   ##no source attribute in S to control printout like R, but
   ##still, stash it here
   mm<-match.call()
   mm$expr<-NULL
   mm[[1]]<-as.name("macro")
   attr(ff,"source")<-c(deparse(mm),deparse(expr))

   ## return the 'macro'
   ff
}
}

Usage Examples from the column:

setNA <- defmacro(df,var,values=-9,expr={df$var[df$var==values] <- NA })
mul <- defmacro(a,b,expr={a*b})

Example using local variables:
mul <- defmacro(a,b,expr={result <- a*b; result},local="result")

----------------

Finally, my original question:

From: Gary Sabot <gary at sabot.com>
Sender: s-news-owner at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
To: s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
Subject: [S] S and macros
Date: Thu, 3 Oct 2002 07:53:09 -0400

I know that S has a variety of functionality that allows you to
compute on the language itself like deparse, substitute etc.  So you
can compute expressions, evaluate them, etc.  I was wondering if
anyone has used that to develop any sort of substitution macro
facility in S or R.  I was hoping for something as powerful as
defmacro/backquote in lisp, but even something with the minimal
functionality of define/cpp as used in C would be helpful.

Here are two sample cases to illustrate the flavor of the problems I
would like to address:

1.  Frequently I want to return a list of objects, and have the list
    names match the objects, i.e.

    list(obj1=obj1,
         obj2=obj2,
         obj3=obj3)

    etc.

    This is redundant, prone to typo/cut/paste errors if names are
    similar (i.e. an obj3=obj2 might sneak in), prone to error not
    caught by the S parser if commas are missing, etc.  Certainly you
    could write something in S to construction the expression above
    and then evaluate it, or to assign names after the fact, but I'm
    looking for something more pattern based that would address this
    and other issues as well.

    This kind of thing can be defined more elegantly with lisp
    backquote, but even cpp can do something useful:

    #define doubleup(x) x=x
    list(doubleup(obj1),
         doubleup(obj2),
         doubleup(obj3))

    Or in a bizarre combination of S, C, and Lisp:
    #define doubleup(x) x=x
    #define namedlist(objects) list(,@lapply(objects,doubleup)
    namedlist(obj1,obj2,obj3)

2. Perhaps you have written a large function and you recognize that
   some sections of it are near copies of each other and should be
   abstracted out to a new subfunction.  You might find that the
   section you are abstracting has many ties via many variables to the
   environment of the parent, and everyone of them must be passed down
   to the subfunction (as well as the possible fun of dealing with the
   semantics of "...").  Below is a trivial example using + (pretend
   instead that it does something complicated, not something simple
   and commutative like +; perhaps it is a simulation depending on all
   5 args or something), you might start out with this in the big
   function body:

     #pretend each line is really 50 lines of code doing a complicated
     #simulation that depends on all 5 of its inputs
     a <- a + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5
     b <- b + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5

   If that took up 100 lines of code, you might instead turn it into 2
   lines and then a 50 line function that gets used twice:

     a <- subfunc(a,temp2,temp3,temp4,temp5)
     b <- subfunc(b,temp2,temp3,temp4,temp5)

     subfunc <- function(x,temp2,temp3,temp4,temp5) {
        x + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5
     }

   This can certainly shorten the function and reduce the amount of
   code that appears twice, since it is abstracted into subfunc.
   However, it requires you to define subfunc with all those args, and
   in editing to create subfunc there are many cut/paste errors you
   might make (leaving a.temp1 in place).  Some cut/paste errors get
   caught at run time when the variable is undefined, but others might
   find a value and return a bad result.

   I would rather do something involving text/rewriting/macro where
   the function call semantics do not come into play, i.e.

     #define pattern(x) x <- x + temp2 + temp3 + temp4 + temp5
     pattern(a)
     pattern(b)

Any suggestions?  Maybe these kinds of things can be done easily in S
without adding anything as bulky as a function library implementing
some kind of substitution macro, and I'm just not thinking about this
the right way?

Thanks.

--garyg

QUESTION:

> 
> 2) Y-axis: Is on a log base 10 scale, from 0-20.

> or a legend.

>

-----Original Message-----
From: Dimitris Rizopoulos [mailto:jimsailgr at yahoo.gr]
Sent: Saturday, October 05, 2002 3:29 AM
To: Kurbat, Matt
Subject: Re: [S] graphing question

Dear Matt,

try something like the following:

data <- data.frame(year=rep(1988:2002, rep(12,
length(1988:2002))), month=rep(1:12, length(1988:2002)),
x1=sort(rnorm(180, 200)), x2=sort(rnorm(180, 200)),
x3=sort(rnorm(180, 200)))
data$lab <- paste(data[,2], "/",data[,1], sep="")
plot(1:180, y=log(data$x1, base=10), type="n", axes=F,
xlab="months", ylab="log-scale")
axis(1, at=1:180, labels=data$lab)
axis(2)
lines(log(data$x1, base=10), col=2)
lines(log(data$x2, base=10), col=3)
lines(log(data$x3, base=10), col=4)
key(x=10, text=names(data)[3:5], lines=list(col=2:4))

I hope this helps.

Best,
Dimitris

RESPONSE #2

You can't do a log scale from zero. Log(0) is undefined. There is no such 
number x such that exp(x)=0. You have to choose an arbitrarily small number, 
e.g. 0.01, instead. 
 
Regarding the axes:
labels.txt <- "1/"+seq(1988:2002)
xticks <- 1988:2002
axis(1,at=xticks, labels=labels.txt)
 
For the last question you have to produce some code and some more details.
 
Yours, Jan Brogger

messages.body_plain:
Replies were rapid and succinct as usual. All suggested 
the use of either on.exit or on.error to close the filehandle. on.exit works 
perfectly in my case, but (perhaps surprisingly) on.error 
doesn't. Trying out on.error also periodically crashed S-plus and I even 
got an 'Engine connection failure' at one point. Note that this applies to 
Script files. Functions quite possibly behave differently.

 

A 
function call to allConnections() from the command line following an aborted 
script didn't appear to return the unclosed file.

 

Wrapping the script as a function would probably 
offer some other alternatives as well but the script interface is preferable in 
my case and on.exit appears to work reliably.

 

Thanks,

 

Steve

messages.subject: Summary: nice dot plot
messages.body_plain:
Yesterday I asked the following question:

"Does anyone has a (pointer to 
a) function producing 'nice' dot plots, that is 

those in which (nearly) tied points 
are displayed in a direction orthogonal to 

the scale as non-overlapping adjacent 
dots? "

Thanks to all who responded. 

Terry Therneau pointed to his "jitplot" 
function 

in http://www.mayo.edu/hsr/Sfunc.html. 

This function can indeed produce nice 
dot plots (vs a group variable). 

David Parkhurst sent in his dp.dotplot() 
which is listed below.

Several persons have suggested to 
use stripplot() with jitter=T, 

or to use the function jitter(). Although 
random dot displacement 

does increase the visibility of separate 
points, many people 

prefer neatly ordered points. 

See http://www.spss.com/research/wilkinson/Publications/dots.pdf 

for more info on construction of such 
nice dot plots.

Thanks for help,

Vaclav Fidler

Response of David Parkhurst:

This function worked the last I tried 
it.  I hope it is well enough 
documented.  It

allows plotting more than one variable, 
in vertically stacked plots.

Dave Parkhurst

x,

  #print(x)

used for adjusted plot data

  xx _ array(rep(0,nr*nc),c(nr,nc))

  yy _ array(rep(0,nr*nc),c(nr,nc))

#print("Just before start of 
loop 1")

# Next part seems to assume there 
are some positive numbers

  for (i in 1:nr) { # Step through 
rows to set up plot data     #1

                    # 
For now, ignore y offset for each group

    m _ min(as.numeric(x[i,]), 
na.rm=T)*0.999999

na.rm=T)

 if (m==0) m_-0.05*M        ##### 
Experimenting (2/22/01)---worked

messages.subject: Re: shift and scale distribution
messages.body_plain:
Dear Weijie,

At 12:04 PM 10/9/2002 -0400, Weijie Cai wrote:

> I generated a set of random variables by a certain probability density
> function, (it is not a common distribution), it is not symmetric, now I
> want to shift it to make its median=0 (not mean) and scale it to make its
> variance=4, how to do it?

Unless I misunderstand what you have and what you want, subtracting the 
current median will make the median 0; likewise, dividing by the current 
standard deviation and multiplying by 2 will make the variance 4.

I hope that this helps,
 John

messages.subject_clean: Finding if an hour belongs to an event - Question of efficiency
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all who provided their answers (below) - and there were plenty of
good ones:

Bill Dunlap (whose second of two solutions I followed), Nick Lacantore,
Jingshang Zhang(based on a small loop), Nick Ellis, Xueer Li, Dimitris
Rizopoulos, & Patrick Burns

Here is the original question:
> I am trying to avoid the (double) loop in the exercise below.  Any good
ideas?
> Assume 3 vectors:
> HoursOfYear <- seq(1:8760)
>
> and these event vectors:
> eventStarts <- c(6,90,1420,8700)
> eventEnds <- c(7,  92, 1425, 8720)
> (i.e. I have 4 events in this case:  one lasting from hour 6 of the year
tohour 7,
> another from hour 90 to hour 92, another from hour > 1420 to 1425 and
> the last one from hour 8700 to 8720)
> Normally the latter two would have a length of 30-60.
>
> I want to create a data frame with two columns
> eventTable <- data.frame(HoursOfYear, InEvent)
> the InEvent vector will be True or False, depending on
> whether an hour is within the span of an event's life.
> For example:
> HoursOfYear InEvent
> 1           F
> 2           F
> 3           F
> ...
> 6           T
> 7           T
> 8           F
> ...
>
> Is there a function that would help me do that?

Bill Dunlap
The following 2 functions do close to what I think you want.  The second is
more efficient when there are lots of intervals to check, but is trickier
to understand.  Neither loops over x so both a pretty fast unless there are
a lot of intervals.  They both allow overlapping intervals and return the
number of
intervals each value in x is in.  (In Splus 0 is equivalent to FALSE).

E.g., on a Sun Sparc Utlra-250 with length(x)=10000 and 50 intervals
f0 took 0.28 seconds and f1 took 0.08.  If there are missing values
in x then f1 will give the wrong answers but could be patched up to
handle them.

"f0" <-
function(x, start, stop)
{
        # for each x count how many start-stop intervals it is in.
        # Assume interval is closed at the bottom and open at top.
             # Change the >= and < in loop to change that.
        if(length(start) != length(stop))
                stop("length(start) != length(stop)")
        if(!all(start <= stop))
                stop("!all(start<stop)")
        val <- rep(0, length(x))
        for(i in seq(along = start))
                val <- val + (x >= start[i] & x < stop[i])
        val
}

"f1" <-
function(x, start, stop)
{
        # for each x count how many start-stop intervals it is in.
        # Assume interval is closed at the bottom and open at top.
        # Rearrange the (start, stop, x) and the (1,-1,0) to change that.
        if(length(start) != length(stop)) stop("length(start) !=
length(stop)")
        if(!all(start <= stop))
                stop("!all(start<stop)")
        if(length(start) == 0)
                return(rep(0, length(x)))
        i <- order(c(start, stop, x))
        cumsum(rep(c(1, -1, 0), c(length(start), length(stop), length(x)))[
                i])[order(i)][ - (1:(2 * length(start)))]
}
---------------------------
Nick Lacantore
In fact, the way you construct the problem, no loop is needed.  You
can construct the vector of T's using paste and eval:

a <- paste(eventStarts, eventEnds, sep=':')
b <- paste(a, collapse=',')
trus <- paste("InEvent[c(", b, ")] <- T", sep="")

InEvent <- rep(F, length(HoursOfYear))
eval(parse(text=trus))
new.df <- data.frame(HoursOfYear, InEvent)
print(new.df[1:10,])
------------------------

Yuying Gao

Nick Ellis
Here's one way to do it without loops. I've made the example smaller for
convenience. The trick is to split the numbers 1:n into start groups and
end
groups, then match them up. This exploits the fact that your HoursOfYear is
a regular sequence.

n <- 100
eventStarts <- c(6,  9, 32, 80)
eventEnds <- c(7,  10, 35, 88)
k <- length(eventStarts)+1
endGroup <- rep(1:k,diff(c(0,eventEnds,n)))
startGroup <- rep(1:k-1,diff(c(0,eventStarts-1,n)))
rbind(startGroup,endGroup,InEvent=startGroup==endGroup)

-----------------------------------

==1|eventTable[,5]==1)
eventTable_eventTable[,c(1,6)]
names(eventTable)_c("HoursOfYear","InEvent")
-----------------------------------
Dimitris Rizopoulos
HoursOfYear <- seq(1:8760)
eventStarts <- c(6,90,1420,8700)
eventEnds <- c(7,  92, 1425, 8720)
#################
event <- paste(eventStarts, ":", eventEnds, sep="")
event <- unlist(lapply(1:length(eventEnds), function(i)
eval(parse(text=event[i]))))
InEvent <- replace(rep(F, length(HoursOfYear)), event, T)
eventTable <- data.frame(HoursOfYear, InEvent)
----------------------------
Patrick Burns
I don't have all the details, but my plan would start with interleaving
the start and end times by doing as.vector(rbind(start, end))
add the first and last times onto this.
Then use "rep" and "diff" to get a vector that is TRUE or FALSE for each
hour of the year.  The following command is not right,

Job Specification for Time Series Econometrician/Statistician (PhD)

COMPANY PROFILE

Initiaitve Media Worldwide, part of the Interpublic Group, is the largest
media company in the world with over $22.7billion in billings.  With over
86 offices in 45 countries IM represents the broadest media network, and
its position amongst the top 3 media buyers in each region ensures there
are no weak links in our exhaustive country coverage.  The strength in
depth of Initiatives' network is reinforced by the fact that 75% of our
business is from multi-national advertisers, who cover all sectors ranging
from Unilever and Johnson & Johnson through PwC, Cisco Systems and GM.

I-Consulting  (I-C)  is  the  Initiative  Group's econometric modelling and
marketing  consultancy  division.   I-C is a global business that leads the
field in terms of econometric modelling.

I-CONSULTING

I-C  enjoys  a  very specific status providing high-end strategic marketing
consultancy  to both Initiative Media and non-Initiative Media clients, and
is   one  of  their  premium  brands.   Its  consultancy  services  include
market-mix  analysis,  investment  prioritisation, return-on-investment and
econometric  modelling.  I-C  has formulated a unique and advanced approach
and  is  able  to  mix  sophisticated  statistical  knowledge  with  market
understanding  and presentation skills, providing the client group with the
ability to measure and analyse their marketing mix.

In  2001 I-C delivered over 25 projects for a number of multi-national blue
chip advertisers, including high profile brands such as Pepsico, Kellogg's,
Unilever,  Sony, Motorola, Peugeot, Shell, Del Monte ? to name a few.   I-C
also participated in a number of international pitches and its contribution
to   the  positioning  of  Initiative  Media  as  a  leading  communication
management group has proven invaluable.

The  main I-C offices are in New York, London and Athens (Omega). The Omega
centre  is  responsible  for  most  of  the  technical  analysis  conducted
worldwide.

The  team  is  lead by Dr. Hans Jessen, President of I-C.  An International
expert in this field, Hans finished his PhD in Econometrics and started his
career  as  Assistant  Professor at the Manchester Metropolitan University.
After  five  years  in academia he moved to Millward Brown International as
Head  of  Statistics and Sampling.  He joined Initiative Media's Consulting
group three years ago and is now President of I-C.  Hans has also consulted
for  a  large number of leading global organisations on their marketing and
media  strategies  and  has  worked as an advisor for both the OECD and the
European Union's Statistical Office.  He is a journal referee for the Royal
Economic  Society,  the  Royal  Statistical  Society  and the International
Journal of Computational Economics.

The  team  that  Dr. Jessen has built includes consultants, econometricians
and  statisticians  with further hires planned this year in line with I-C's
ambitious  growth  plans.   As  part of that growth, there is now a need to
take  on a new Senior Time Series Econometrician/Statistician for the Omega
Centre.

THE REQUIREMENT

The  Senior  Time Series Econometrician/Statistician, will initially report
directly  to  Dr. Hans Jessen. The new senior person will work as part of a
very  strong technical team of econometricians and statisticians conducting
multinational projects for leading companies. Most of the work will involve
time  series  regression models and it is important that the person is very
strong  both theoretically and in applied regression. The analysis is based
on  S-Plus  - expert knowledge is not required although it is an advantage.
It  is  required  that  the person is educated to PhD level and has already
done any potential military service. The position is permanent and based in
Athens  but  we  expect  some international travel (mainly Europe) and also
that the person is willing to work flexible hours.

This  is an exceptional opportunity for the right person to play a key role

messages.subject: Re: tapply for matrices
messages.body_plain:
Tony Plate provided what seems to be a very fast and elegant solution - see 
below.  I have modified his solution slightly:

mapply <- function(X, INDEX, FUN=NULL, ..., simplify=TRUE) {
## Matrix tapply
## X: matrix with n rows; INDEX: vector or list of vectors of length n
## FUN: function to operate on submatrices of x by INDEX
## ...: arguments to FUN; simplify: see sapply
## Modification of code by Tony Plate <tplate at blackmesacapital.com> 10Oct02
idx.list <- tapply(seq(nrow(X)), INDEX, c)
sapply(idx.list, function(idx,x,fun,...) fun(x[idx,,drop=FALSE],...),
       x=X, fun=FUN, ..., simplify=simplify)
}

Example: mapply(x, groups, quantile, probs=c(.25,.5)) will create a matrix of 
first and second quartiles of submatrices of x grouped by groups.

The usages I have for this right now are certain within-subject bivariate 
summaries when subjects have multiple rows of data.

Thanks Tony,

Frank

P.S.  Dave Krantz <dhk at paradox.psych.columbia.edu> reported that he wrote a 
function mtapply that uses for loops for this but that pays a lot of attention 
to formatting the output as an array with sensible dimnames.

Tony Plate <tplate at blackmesacapital.com> wrote:

> 
> idx.list <- tapply(seq(numRows(x)), x[,grouping.variable], c)
> lapply(idx.list, function(idx, x) {
>     submatrix <- x[idx,,drop=F]
>     ... operate on submatrix ...
> }, x)
> 
> which seems pretty fast.  I sometimes sort x beforehand so that rows with

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

On a related note, I am a Newbie, and have written the
following function (below) as a much quicker alternative to
aggregate(). I wrote it because aggregate() seems to bog down
severely on the larger data frames that I work with (let's say
5000 x 50), and when the index variable has many levels, and when
multiple variables are used as indices. My version is just
combining tapply and sapply...

As far as I can tell, the only difference (aside from not
having methods for ts and/or other objects yet), is that my
function doesn't add columns containing the index variable(s)
in the output. (This can easily be added).

Perhaps people can comment on why the approach I've taken
may not be a good one (so that I can improve it, and learn more
about writing functions in general).

Thanks in advance for any suggestions or comments!

Cheers,

Rob

ag.fast <- function(x,by=NULL,FUN=NULL,...) {

 if(is.null(FUN)) stop("You need to specify a legitimate function.")
 FUN <- match.fun(FUN)
 n <- length(by)
 if(n==1)
   int <- by[1]
 else
   int <- interaction(by[1:n], drop=T)

 f <- function(x, FUN,...) {
   tapply(x,int,FUN,...)
  }

 x <- x[,1:ncol(x)]
 s <- sapply(x,f,FUN,...)
 s <- data.frame(cbind(s[,c(1:ncol(s))]))
 return(s)

}

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Sundar Dorai-Raj of PDF Solutions who provided the following code 
to extract the estimated variance components from an nlme object:

extract.stdev <- function(object) {
struct <- object$modelStruct$reStruct
sigma <- object$sigma
Var <- rev(sapply(struct, as.matrix))
labels <- sapply(seq(Var), function(x, names)
paste(rev(names[1:x]), collapse = " %in% "), names = names(Var))
Sdev <- c(sqrt(Var) * sigma, sigma)
names(Sdev) <- c(labels, "Residual")
Sdev
}

ORIGINAL POST:
My organization has recently gotten involved with microarray analysis.  
Our biologists would prefer that the data be analyzed in-house.  I have 
been assigned the task of getting our department up to speed on microarray 
data analysis techniques.  My training is in the area of statistics, and 
I have three questions:

(1)  Does anyone know of a good workshop where the basics of microarray
statistical analysis are taught?

(2)  What would be a good book, for a statistician, to read to teach himself
(or herself) the basics of microarray analysis?

(3)  How well do the cclust, cluster, mclust, multiv, affy, BioConductor,
CyberT, GeneSOM, mixture modelling, PAM, permax, OOMAL, R/maanova, SMA, 
SMA extension, Spot, and YASMA packages for R perform w.r.t. microarray 
database size and w.r.t. the sophistication of commercially available 
microarray analysis packages?  The author of the website 
http://ihome.cuhk.edu.hk/~b400559/arraysoft_rpackages.html  personally
recommends R as a good choice for microarray analysis, with the above 
mentioned downloadable packages added in.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
ANSWER #1:

david> My organization has recently gotten involved with
    david> microarray analysis.  Our biologists would prefer that the
    david> data be analyzed in-house.  I have been assigned the task
    david> of getting our department up to speed on microarray data
    david> analysis techniques.  My training is in the area of
    david> statistics, and I have three questions:

    david> (1) Does anyone know of a good workshop where the basics of
    david> microarray statistical analysis are taught?

You might ask on the Bioconductor list.  We've got Robert G. coming
out to talk at FHCRC in Seattle; I don't think there is any space
left, though.  It's reasonably cheap, if you've got a group that wants
training.

    david> (2) What would be a good book, for a statistician, to read
    david> to teach himself (or herself) the basics of microarray
    david> analysis?

Good question: 3 basic techniques are important to understand:
normalization, "differential expression", and clustering.  As far as I
know, your group knows a good bit about the last; the second is the
multiple comparisons problem, i.e. how to figure out which t
statistics are critical when you've got thousands of them.  The first
is just making sure that with lots of noise and variability, that
there is some hope of comparing across chip.

As far as books go, there are a few coming out, but none I'd
particular recommend (or recommend against).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------
ANSWER #2:

Paul,

We are offering a two-day R/Splus microarray course in Boston
October 24-25. This course is taught by Prof Vince Carey
who is a Bioconductor developer.

If you are interested in this course, please let me know.

I look forward to hearing for you.

Cheers,
Elvis Miller, Ph.D

messages.subject: Re: software for skewed data
messages.body_plain:
CT

The reason I am surprised that you are asking this question is that there is no single answer or coherent set of answers to your problem and therefore no single program to deal with it.  Any statistical approach for skewed data must confront a variety of reasons for the skewness.  There are at least five I can immediately think of.

First, the sample may be slightly skewed through sampling fluctuations, in which case nothing may need to be done. The standard linear model is robust against moderate skewness in large samples.

Second, the sample may be transformed from a skewed sample to a more symmetric one.  Then one analyzes the transformed data.  There is one called the Box-Cox transformation than can be used to select a large family of transformations. Is this what you are asking about?

Third, one may use a non-parametric analysis. These methods often handle skewed data quite well.

Fourth, the distribution (not sample) may be confined to the positive reals. Then you need a statistical model, and there are lots of them, that addresses this type of distribution.

Fifth, the data may be a mixture of distributions so that the skewness is caused by a primary distribution occasionally contaminated by a secondary distribution.

There are probably other heterogeneous reasons for skewness. So, IMHO, a statistical package specific to skewed data makes no sense.

Joe

messages.subject: Shapiro-Wilk's (or Shapiro-Francia) for small samples?
messages.body_plain:
Dear group,

I am using the attached program to perform a Shapiro-Wilks' test on
a sample of size 29. I believe that the program was taken from
Statlib. Well, the p-value gets reported as zero. I wanted to check
out the test myself. So I obtained 1000 samples of size 29 from N(0,1)
and ran the test 1000 times. In each case, I got a p-value of the test
statistic to be 0.

I then ran the same experiment with a sample of size 50. Only in 16
cases (1.6%) did I get a p-value of greater than 0.05. For sample
sizes 100, 200, and 500, the proportion of cases was 47.4%, 62.83% and
72%. Does that mean that the Shapiro-Wilks is unreliable at lower
sample sizes like 29? What alternative avenues are available to test
here? Is the Shapiro-Francia test preferred?

Thanks and best wishes,
Ranjan

messages.subject: Re: modeling log transformed values in lme
messages.subject_clean: modeling log transformed values in lme
messages.body_plain:
Buzz Burhans asks:

>  -----Original Message-----
> From:         Buzz Burhans [mailto:wsb2 at cornell.edu] 
> Sent: Thursday, October 17, 2002 5:47 AM
> To:   s-news at lists-new.biostat.wustl.edu
> Subject:      modeling log transformed values in lme
> 
> I would appreciate some advice on how to deal with data which is not
> normally distributed, but which could be rendered normally distributed if
> log transformed. 
        [WNV]  I take it you mean that after log transformation of the data
the residuals appear more normally distributed, after fitting appropriate
linear models.

>  the data is reflects both fixed and random effects, so I would like to
> use lme. however, am I correct in that there is no capability in lme to
> use a log-link model? 
        [WNV]  No, there is not, and if your statement above is correct you
don't want a log link.  With a log link you will be fitting a model with
that has additive, homoscedastic errors but with a multiplicative mean
structure.  It sounds like you have a multiplicative error structure as well
which requires a log transformation of the data to turn it into an additive,
homoscedastic one.

> It seems my alternatives with this data are to either transform it to
> logged values and model the logged values with lme, or to use the raw
> values and model it with nlme?  If this is the case, which is the
> preferable approach, using lme with log transformed values, or using nlme?
        [WNV]  it all hinges on the error structure.  If you have a
multiplicative error structure (in my experience by far the usual case) you
should transform and use lme, if you have a multiplicative mean structure
but an additive, homoscedastic error structure, you should use either nlme
or the function glmmPQL from the MASS4 library.  I'd be surprised if you
need the latter, but of course the former is problematical if you have some
rogue zeros in the data.  Avoid the temptation to "add a little bit" and
then transform and pretend nothing happened.  Please.

> Thanks
> 
> Buzz Burhans
> Dept. of Animal Science
> Cornell University
>

>
>   -----Original Message-----
> From: Lucke, Joseph F
>   [mailto:LUCKE at uthscsa.edu]
> Sent: Wednesday, October 16, 2002 11:10
>   PM
> To: 'Chi-tsung Wu'; jagadish rangrej;
>   charles.anderson at dnr.state.mn.us; Lucke, Joseph F; andy_liaw at merck.com;
>   s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
> Subject: RE: [S] software for skewed
>   data
>
>
>
>   CT
>
>   The reason I am surprised that you are asking this question is
>   that there is no single answer or coherent set of answers to your problem and
>   therefore no single program to deal with it.  Any statistical approach
>   for skewed data must confront a variety of reasons for the skewness.
>   There are at least five I can immediately think of.
>
>   First, the sample may be slightly skewed through sampling
>   fluctuations, in which case nothing may need to be done. The standard linear
>   model is robust against moderate skewness in large samples.
>
>   Second, the sample may be transformed from a skewed sample to
>   a more symmetric one.  Then one analyzes the transformed data.
>   There is one called the Box-Cox transformation than can be used to select a
>   large family of transformations. Is this what you are asking about?
>
>   Third, one may use a non-parametric analysis. These methods
>   often handle skewed data quite well.
>
>   Fourth, the distribution (not sample) may be confined to the
>   positive reals. Then you need a statistical model, and there are lots of them,
>   that addresses this type of distribution.
>
>   Fifth, the data may be a mixture of distributions so that the
>   skewness is caused by a primary distribution occasionally contaminated by a
>   secondary distribution.
>
>   There are probably other heterogeneous reasons for skewness.
>   So, IMHO, a statistical package specific to skewed data makes no
>   sense.
>
>   Joe
>
>

Carroll R.J. et Ruppert D., 1988, Transformation and weighting in Regression, London, Chapman & Hall.

what would be the difference between lme and nlme in case you have a lot of zeros in a non-negative y? Don't we add more than a little bit when we tranform y in lme (e.g. log(y+1))?

Frédéric Gosselin

Ranjan,

included in S-PLUS 6.1.  I tried both versions on the data and got
different answers.  Here's my output:
> x <-rnorm(29)
> shapiro.test(x)

      Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test

data:  x

$W:
[1] 0.9391132

$n:
[1] 29

$p:
[1] 0

  As you can see, even the W statistic is slightly different.  I tried it
several times and there was always a substantial difference between the
two.
Dave

messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

I?m working on a project which aims to relate the appearance of
fungus (binary response: Iasi) with several demographic (age,
BMI) and environmental (C1, C2) variables. The data were
collected in 2 hospitals. My intention is to draw inference for
the entire population of hospitals, so I want to use GLMM.

When I try the following fixed-effects glm I see that there are
no statistical differences between the 2 hospitals:

model.0<-glm(Iasi~age+BMI+C1+C2+hosp, family=binomial, data=dat)

dropterm(model.0, test = "Chisq")

Single term deletions

<none>    169.2972 181.2972

    C1  1 172.6438 182.6438  3.34664 0.0673421
    C2  1 203.8095 213.8095 34.51230 0.0000000
  hosp  1 169.5270 179.5270  0.22980 0.6316693

new MASS library I get the following results:

model.1<-glmmPQL(Iasi~age+BMI+C1+C2, random=~1|hosp,
family=binomial, data=dat)

I see that CI for the variance component of the random-effect is
